newsitem.title: USA: U.S. supports Canada plan for Zaire force HQ.
newsitem.headline: U.S. supports Canada plan for Zaire force HQ.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday it supported a Canadian proposal to set up a headquarters for an international force to ease the refugee crisis in Zaire.

The White House also said in a statement that it was putting personnel on alert possibly to take part in airdrops of food to Rwandan refugees in Zaire but it said it had not made a final decion on whether to participate in the airdrops.

"The United States welcomes Canada's proposal to establish the multinational headquarters for the planned humanitarian mission in Central Africa," the White House said. "The mission would be to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance and ... the return of refugees to Rwanda."
The statement added that the United States was working with Canada and others to plan for airdrops in Zaire, saying this was expected to take several days.
"Once that planning is complete, we expect to make a final decision as to what can be accomplished effectively and what precise role the U.S. will play in this effort.

"In the meantime, the U.S. is putting personnel on alert for potential airdrop operations and taking other steps that would enable the U.S. to respond swiftly in the event that airdrops are required," it said.
Canada, impatient with international indecision over the multilateral force approved by the United Nations on Nov. 15, proposed on Tuesday that it be based at Entebbe, Uganda.

Western military leaders agreed in Stuttgart, Germany, last weekend, that the mission would be limited to delivering aid and bringing home the thousands of refugees, most of them Rwandans who fled civil war in their homeland in 1994.
The White House said Washington would contribute personnel to the multilateral force headquarters as well as providing airlift, air control and other services.

"We look forward to working with the government of Canada over the next couple of days to finalise the details of the mission, including establishing a political oversight group for the mission ... (and) obtaining the necessary consent of the governments in the region," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns added in his daily news briefing.
Burns said Washington wanted to see "significant African participation" in the force and that the rules of engagement needed to be defined.

Earlier on Wednesday, Defence Secretary William Perry said Washington was ready to take part in the airdrops but he told reporters accompanying him to Naples, Italy, that there was no question of sending a U.S. combat force to Zaire.
